title: The Half-Light Interior
premise: August Thackeray has spent forty years tuning pianos in the fading resort town of Vellamook, listening to the half-light between what people say and what they mean, while guarding the secret that they were born into the Thackeray family as the child no one wanted to acknowledge. When Ilsa Renner, the last fluent speaker of Vellamook's dying immigrant tongue, asks August to become her final student, the lessons force open the family's arranged silence—especially around August's mother, Vivian, who traded her own fluency for respectability and her child's invisibility for survival. As Ilsa declines and Vivian's health fails, August must finally ask why the family chose erasure over love, learning that the answer was never shame but a bargain made in fear. The novel ends with Ilsa's death, August speaking her eulogy in a language only two people alive ever shared, and choosing at last to be seen.
about_author: Cyrus Whitlock is the pen name of a former piano restorer who spent two decades working in coastal towns before turning to fiction. Their stories examine quiet lives and the languages—spoken and unspoken—that families invent to survive themselves.

chapters.title: The Radiator Archive
chapters.summary: August tunes the piano in the shuttered Grand Hotel, cataloguing the house's sounds and its unsaid things. A brief flashback establishes their habit of invisibility within the Thackeray family. POV: August. Emotional beat: melancholy competence—the comfort and cost of being unheard.

chapters.title: A Woman Who Counts Her Words
chapters.summary: Ilsa Renner summons August to tune her upright piano and, mid-appointment, begins counting aloud in a language August almost recognizes from childhood. She announces she wants one final student before she dies. POV: August. Emotional beat: startled recognition, like hearing your own name in a crowd.

chapters.title: Vivian's Silence
chapters.summary: August visits their mother Vivian, now frail, and mentions Ilsa; Vivian's reaction is swift, cold refusal. Through fragmented memory we learn August once knew words of the old tongue and was made to forget them. POV: August. Emotional beat: dread—the past pressing against a sealed door.

chapters.title: First Lessons
chapters.summary: Against Vivian's wishes, August begins lessons with Ilsa, who teaches through objects, songs, and scoldings rather than grammar. Each recovered word unsettles something in August's body memory. POV: August. Emotional beat: tentative joy shadowed by guilt, like stealing warmth.

chapters.title: The Bargain of 1968
chapters.summary: An aunt, Marguerite, reveals part of the family history: Vivian gave up the language and her community ties to marry into respectability, and August's existence was kept quiet to protect the marriage. POV shifts to Marguerite. Emotional beat: uneasy sympathy—she believes she is defending Vivian, not betraying August.

chapters.title: What the Piano Remembers
chapters.summary: Tuning an old instrument in the Thackeray house, August finds sheet music annotated in the dying language—Vivian's handwriting—and realizes her silence was practiced daily, a performance renewed for decades. POV: August. Emotional beat: grief reframing anger; the enemy becomes a fellow prisoner.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Kitchen Table
chapters.summary: August finally asks Vivian the question the whole family arranged itself around: why erasure instead of love? Vivian, lucid for one fierce hour, tells the truth—a threat, a deportation order, a choice between the language and her child's safety. POV alternates August/Vivian. Emotional beat: the climax; devastation and release entangled.

chapters.title: Ilsa's Last Word
chapters.summary: Ilsa's health collapses; from her hospital bed she drills August on the funeral blessing, insisting the language must outlive her mouth. August resists becoming a monument, then accepts. POV: August. Emotional beat: tender urgency—love expressed as transmission, not possession.

chapters.title: The Eulogy
chapters.summary: At Ilsa's funeral, August rises and speaks in the old tongue before the stunned town, then translates deliberately, publicly claiming both the language and their own hidden history. Vivian attends in a wheelchair and does not look away. POV: August. Emotional beat: exposure as liberation; terror transfigured into witness.

chapters.title: Half-Light, Whole Voice
chapters.summary: Months later, August keeps the hotel piano tuned, teaches three curious children Ilsa's words, and sits with Vivian practicing vocabulary without apology or explanation. The inventory of unsaid things is finally, imperfectly, spoken. POV: August. Emotional beat: quiet resolution—inheritance reclaimed, survival redefined as presence.
